questions.q: What problem does integration documentation directly solve, per this lesson's connection back to Lesson 17?
options: It eliminates the need for any monitoring
It moves design knowledge out of individual people's heads into a durable, findable artifact, directly fixing the "nobody knows what this integration does anymore" governance failure
It replaces the need for an architecture review
It is purely a legal requirement with no practical governance value
questions.explain: Documentation is the concrete fix for the governance failure described in Lesson 17 — it makes the reasoning behind a design durable and findable instead of living only in the memory of whoever built it.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed among the seven sections this lesson says a real integration design document should contain?
options: The exact dollar amount the integration project cost to build
A list of every unrelated integration in the organization
The personal phone number of the original developer
Pattern and justification — which pattern was chosen and why, referencing the specific facts that drove the choice
questions.explain: Pattern and justification is one of the seven sections: documenting not just which pattern was chosen but the specific reasoning (tied to Lesson 11's four questions) behind that choice, so a future reader can judge whether it still holds.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the "failure handling" section of a document should cover idempotency, retry strategy, and dead-letter destination?
options: Because these are the exact failure-handling concepts covered in Lessons 15 and 16, and writing them down lets a future reader know how the integration behaves when something goes wrong without having to reverse-engineer it
Because these details are purely optional and rarely matter in practice
Because only synchronous integrations need this section documented
Because dead-letter destinations never need to be known by anyone but the original developer
questions.explain: The failure-handling section captures exactly the Lesson 15 and Lesson 16 concepts (idempotency, retry/backoff/jitter, dead-letter destination) so a future reader can understand the integration's failure behavior from the document rather than having to reconstruct it.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say stale documentation can be worse than no documentation at all?
options: Because stale documentation always contains deliberately false information
Because stale documentation takes up more storage space than no documentation

Because a future engineer trusting an outdated description (such as an old retry strategy or an incorrect field-ownership claim) can make a confidently wrong decision based on information that used to be true
Because stale documentation is always written in the wrong format
questions.explain: The danger of stale documentation is that it's trusted — a reader acts on outdated information with confidence, making a wrong decision they wouldn't have made with no documentation prompting false certainty at all.

questions.q: What practice does this lesson recommend to prevent a document from going stale?
options: Writing the document once at launch and never revisiting it
Treating a documentation update as part of the definition of "done" for any change to an integration, with the same update discipline as the code or configuration it describes
Deleting documentation entirely once an integration has been running for more than a year
Only updating documentation during an annual audit, regardless of how many changes occurred in between
questions.explain: The lesson recommends treating documentation as a living artifact: a documentation update is part of what it means for a change to an integration to be considered complete, not an optional step squeezed in when convenient.
